sentence: Coeliac disease is a lifelong autoimmune condition in which the immune system reacts to gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley and rye.

sentence: The reaction damages the surface of the small bowel, so the gut cannot absorb nutrients well.

sentence: Coeliac disease commonly causes diarrhoea, stomach aches and bloating.
Indigestion and constipation can also occur, and diarrhoea happens because the small bowel cannot absorb nutrients.
Fatty, foul-smelling stools are also common.
Other effects include tiredness, unplanned weight loss and an itchy rash.
Nerve problems can occur, such as tingling in the hands and feet, and balance or speech difficulties.
Symptoms can range from mild to severe, and they often come and go.
A rash called dermatitis herpetiformis is itchy and blistered, and it typically appears on the elbows, knees and buttocks.
Some people have no symptoms at all, and around 20% of people with the condition are found through tests for other conditions.
note: Search 2 summary states around 20% have no symptoms and are found via tests for other conditions.

sentence: In children, the condition can slow growth and delay puberty.
Coeliac disease is an autoimmune reaction.
The immune system mistakes substances in gluten for a threat to the body and attacks them, which damages the surface of the small bowel.
Gluten is a protein found in wheat, barley and rye.
It is unclear exactly what triggers the reaction.
A mix of genes and the environment seems to play a part.
Research shows that people with the condition carry genes that make them more likely to develop it.
Having a close relative with the condition raises the chance, and one leaflet states that about 1 in 10 blood relatives of a person with coeliac disease also have it.
note: Search 4 leaflet and search 5 NHS causes (approx 10% with family history); attribution partly uncertain.

sentence: Type 1 diabetes is linked with coeliac disease, probably because the two conditions share a genetic risk.
The NHS advises testing for people with ongoing unexplained gut symptoms, unexplained weight loss, long-lasting tiredness, or unexplained iron or vitamin deficiency anaemia.
Testing is also suggested for people with type 1 diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease.
NICE also recommends testing for first-degree relatives of a person with coeliac disease.
note: Search 3 and 8: NICE guideline mentions first-degree relatives.

sentence: The two main methods are a blood test and a biopsy of the small bowel.
A GP arranges the first blood test.
After a positive result the GP refers the person to a gastroenterologist, who may arrange more blood tests or a biopsy in hospital.
The NHS says gluten must stay in the diet until testing is done, because stopping it can cause a false negative and delay diagnosis.
The NHS also warns against starting a gluten-free diet before a specialist confirms the diagnosis.
There is no cure, but a gluten-free diet should help control symptoms and prevent long-term complications.
All sources of gluten are avoided for life.
Foods such as bread, pasta, cereals, biscuits and cakes are avoided unless they are labelled gluten-free.
Newly diagnosed people are usually referred to a dietitian to help adjust and keep the diet balanced.
Digestive symptoms should improve considerably within weeks, although a skin rash can take longer to clear.
Even small amounts of gluten can cause symptoms and raise the risk of complications.
note: Search 1; Coeliac UK leaflet in search 4 says tiny amounts may cause symptoms short term and gut damage longer term.

sentence: Medication can control the rash of dermatitis herpetiformis, but it does not treat other symptoms, so a gluten-free diet remains an essential part of treatment.
NICE recommends a yearly appointment to review symptoms and how well the diet is working.
Oats do not contain gluten, but many people with the condition avoid them because they can be contaminated with other cereals.
note: Search 4 summary of sources; specific page not identified.

sentence: Poor absorption of nutrients can lead to deficiencies, including iron deficiency anaemia and vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia.
Bones can become brittle and weak, which is called osteoporosis.
Cancers linked to coeliac disease include small bowel cancer and some lymphomas, and the NHS says that after some time on a gluten-free diet the risk is the same as in the general population.
In some people the spleen works less well, making infections more likely.
Some people keep having symptoms despite a gluten-free diet.
note: Search 1 review (up to 30% persistent symptoms; figure omitted); Search 7 NICE: consider other causes and gluten exposure.
